intro.en: History taking, examination and resuscitation of the newborn, with the scores, charts and common problems asked in the practical exam.

items.summary: A set order for noting the mother's antenatal course, the delivery events and the baby's first hours, so no exam point is missed.

blocks.title: History of the mother
bullets: Note the mother's name and age, then gravida, para, living children, abortions and prior newborn deaths.
Record the last menstrual period, the expected date of delivery and whether conception was natural or assisted.
Write the period of gestation (POG) with events of the first, second and third trimesters separately.
Ask about medicines taken in pregnancy, gestational diabetes (GDM) and pregnancy induced hypertension (PIH).

blocks.title: History of labour and delivery
bullets: Record the gap between rupture of membranes (ROM) and birth, plus any vaginal bleeding or infection.
Note the mode of birth: vaginal, assisted vaginal or lower segment caesarean section (LSCS), with the reason for it.

blocks.title: History of the baby
bullets: Record date and time of birth, gestation, single or twin birth with twin order, sex and birth weight.
Classify weight for gestation as small (SGA), appropriate (AGA) or large (LGA) for gestational age.
Note whether resuscitation was used: oxygen by blow-by, bag with mask, or tracheal intubation.
Record Apgar scores at 1 minute and 5 minutes and whether newborn reflexes are intact or depressed.
Ask when breastfeeding began after birth and whether stool and urine have passed.
Ask about abnormal features present at birth and about later feeding, family, immunisation and development.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: A healthy infant usually passes stool in the first 24 hours and urine in the first 48 hours.
Always combine the antenatal, birth and postnatal facts before commenting on risk.

viva.q: What obstetric details must you record before examining the baby?
viva.a: Gravida and para, dates, trimester events, drugs, diabetes, hypertension, membrane rupture interval, bleeding, infection and delivery mode.

viva.q: What resuscitation details do you ask about?
viva.a: Whether blow-by oxygen, bag and mask ventilation or intubation was needed, plus Apgar scores at 1 and 5 minutes.

viva.q: By when should a newborn pass stool and urine?
viva.a: Stool within 24 hours of birth and urine within 48 hours; delay beyond that needs assessment.

items.summary: A head to toe check of the infant covering vital signs, growth measures, the fontanelle, the cord and any birth injury.

blocks.title: Before touching the baby
bullets: Wash the hands well, dry them and warm them before handling the infant.
Check warmth, colour, activity and cry while the baby rests undisturbed.

blocks.title: Vital signs
bullets: Count heart rate and respiratory rate and take the temperature.
Look at skin colour, check pulse oximeter readings and test capillary filling time (CFT).

blocks.title: Anthropometry
bullets: Measure head circumference, body length and chest circumference.
Plot birth weight against gestation to label the baby SGA, AGA or LGA.

blocks.title: Head to toe examination
bullets: Feel the anterior fontanelle (AF) and inspect the scalp, face, eyes, ears, mouth and palate.
Examine the neck, chest, heart, lungs, abdomen, genitalia, limbs, hips, spine and skin.
Inspect the umbilical stump: it should show two arteries with one vein.
Look for signs of birth trauma such as bruises, swellings, nerve weakness or fractures.

blocks.title: Gestational age assessment
bullets: In a preterm infant, grade maturity with the New Ballard scoring system.
The score has two parts: physical maturity and neuromuscular maturity.

viva.q: What do you do before touching a newborn?
viva.a: Wash hands thoroughly, dry them and warm them, then observe colour, warmth, activity and cry.

viva.q: What does the normal umbilical cord contain?
viva.a: Two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein.

viva.q: What are the two parts of the New Ballard score?
viva.a: Physical maturity and neuromuscular maturity, used to assess gestation in preterm babies.

items.summary: The standard age and weight cutoffs that define a neonate, prematurity and low birth weight for exams.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: An infant under 28 days of age
Death of the fetus after 22 weeks of gestation or above 500 gm weight
From 22 weeks of gestation until 7 days after birth
From birth until 1 year of age

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Birth between 37 and 41 weeks of gestation
Weight between the 10th and 90th centile for gestation
Weight below the 10th centile for gestation

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The phases of the Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP), 7th edition, are preparation, resuscitation and post-resuscitation care.
Within resuscitation the sequence taught is TABCD: temperature, airway, breathing, circulation and drugs.

viva.q: Define the perinatal period.
viva.a: From 22 weeks of gestation to 7 days after birth.

viva.q: What weight cutoffs define LBW, VLBW and ELBW?
viva.a: LBW below 2500 gm, VLBW below 1500 gm and ELBW below 1000 gm.

viva.q: What are the three phases of NRP resuscitation?
viva.a: Preparation, resuscitation following TABCD, and post-resuscitation care.

unsure: Source lists LGA as birth weight below the 90th centile, which reads as a slip for above the 90th centile, so the LGA row was left out for reviewer confirmation.

title.en: Preparing for resuscitation and cord clamping

items.summary: How to get the team and kit ready before birth and when to delay clamping the cord.

blocks.title: Anticipatory preparation
bullets: Arrange a trained team in advance and run through a pre-resuscitation checklist.
Keep the resuscitation kit ready and test the suction, oxygen, bag, laryngoscope and warmer.

blocks.title: Delayed cord clamping
bullets: In a straightforward preterm birth, wait at least 60 seconds after delivery before clamping.
Carry out deferred clamping even when the mother has human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.

viva.q: What do you check before a high risk delivery?
viva.a: Team roles, a pre-resuscitation checklist and tested suction, oxygen, bag and mask, intubation kit and warmer.

viva.q: How long do you delay cord clamping in an uncomplicated preterm birth?
viva.a: A minimum of 60 seconds after delivery.

title.en: Keeping the newborn warm and routine care

items.summary: Simple steps to stop heat loss at birth and the routine care of a well infant kept with the mother.

blocks.title: Preventing heat loss
bullets: Wipe the infant dry at once and nurse under a radiant warmer or wrap in warm linen.
For a well baby staying with the mother, keep the infant against her skin and dry promptly.
Hold off the first bath until the next day.
After admission to the neonatal unit, take the axillary temperature within 10 minutes.

viva.q: How do you keep a newborn warm at birth?
viva.a: Dry immediately, use a radiant warmer or warm linen, and use maternal skin contact for well babies.

viva.q: When do you bathe the baby and check temperature?
viva.a: Delay the first bath for a day and record axillary temperature within 10 minutes of unit admission.

title.en: Opening the airway and suctioning the newborn

image.brief: Side view of a newborn manikin on a plain background with head in neutral sniffing position, showing a soft suction catheter and a bulb syringe beside it.

credit.author: U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist Seaman Joseph Caballero

items.summary: Clearing the mouth and nose only when needed, with the correct catheter size, depth and suction pressure.

blocks.title: Airway management
bullets: Wipe the mouth and nose clean; suction is not done as a routine in every birth.
Reserve suction, including bulb syringe use, for infants with visible blockage to breathing.
Also suction babies who are going to need positive pressure ventilation (PPV).

blocks.title: Suction technique
bullets: Pass the catheter about 5 cm into the mouth first, then about 3 cm into the nose.
Use a 12 or 14 Fr catheter with pressure below 50 mm Hg, which is below 100 cm of water.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Position and dry the baby before judging whether suction or ventilation is needed.
Excess or deep suctioning can injure the mucosa and slow the heart, so keep it brief.

viva.q: Is routine suctioning recommended at birth?
viva.a: No. Wipe the mouth and nose and suction only for obvious obstruction or before positive pressure ventilation.

viva.q: Which comes first, mouth or nose, and at what depth?
viva.a: Mouth first to about 5 cm, then nose to about 3 cm.

viva.q: What catheter and pressure do you use?
viva.a: A 12 or 14 Fr catheter at under 50 mm Hg, equal to under 100 cm of water.

items.summary: The suction, oxygen, ventilation, intubation, drug and monitoring kit that must be tested before delivery.

blocks.title: Suction and oxygen
bullets: Keep a meconium aspirator, a mechanical suction unit and catheters of 10, 12 and 14 Fr ready.
Have a working oxygen source with tubing and a flow meter.

blocks.title: Bag and mask
bullets: Use self inflating newborn bags of 250 ml and 500 ml with masks sized for term and preterm faces.

blocks.title: Intubation kit
bullets: Keep a laryngoscope with straight blades: size 0 for preterm infants and size 1 for term infants.
For older children use blade 2 between 1 and 10 years and blade 3 above 10 years.
Stock tracheal tubes, a stylet, carbon dioxide detector, suction and adhesive tape.

blocks.title: Drugs and monitoring
bullets: Draw up epinephrine with normal saline and keep naloxone or sterile water at hand.
Keep a pulse oximeter, exhaled carbon dioxide monitor, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) unit and electroencephalogram (EEG) leads where available.

blocks.title: Miscellaneous
bullets: Keep a stopwatch, warm linen, a shoulder roll, gauze, a radiant warmer and a stethoscope.
Add syringes, a 6 Fr feeding tube, 3.5 and 5 F umbilical catheters, a three way tap and gloves.

viva.q: Which suction catheters and bags do you keep ready?
viva.a: Catheters of 10, 12 and 14 Fr with self inflating bags of 250 ml and 500 ml.

viva.q: Which laryngoscope blade for a preterm and a term baby?
viva.a: Blade 0 for preterm infants and blade 1 for term infants.

viva.q: Which drugs must be at the bedside?
viva.a: Epinephrine with normal saline for flushing, plus naloxone or sterile water.

title.en: Endotracheal tube size and fixation depth

items.summary: A weight and gestation chart for choosing the tracheal tube, with the fixation rule and the formula for older children.

blocks.title: Fixation depth
bullets: Fix the tube at 6 plus the weight in kg, read as the mark on the tube.
A 2.5 kg infant takes a 3.5 tube fixed at the 8.5 mark.
For older children, tube size equals age in years plus 16, divided by 4.
Depth from lips or teeth equals 3 times the tube size: a 4 year old takes size 5 fixed at 15 cm.
Children above 8 years should have a cuffed tracheal tube.

viva.q: Which tube for a 2.5 kg baby, and where do you fix it?
viva.a: A 3.5 mm tube fixed at the 8.5 mark, from 6 plus weight in kg.

viva.q: How do you size a tube for older children?
viva.a: Size equals age in years plus 16 divided by 4, with depth three times the size.

viva.q: When do you switch to a cuffed tube?
viva.a: Above 8 years of age.

title.en: Initial steps of resuscitation at birth

image.brief: Front view of a newborn manikin under a radiant warmer on a plain background, showing drying with warm linen and positioning of the head.

items.summary: Four history questions before birth and three checks at birth that decide whether the infant stays with the mother.

blocks.title: Resuscitation oriented history
bullets: Ask the gestation, whether the liquor is clear, how many infants are expected and what extra risks exist.

blocks.title: Three questions at birth
bullets: Is the infant born at term, crying or breathing, and showing good muscle tone.
If any answer is no, start the initial steps under a radiant warmer.
A vigorous infant with clear liquor needs no warmer steps and can stay with the mother under watch.

blocks.title: TABC sequence
bullets: T stands for stopping heat loss by wiping, warming and covering.
A stands for opening the airway by wiping the mouth and nose, without routine suction.
B stands for starting breaths and C for circulation with drugs when indicated.

viva.q: What four facts do you ask before the birth?
viva.a: Gestation, clarity of fluid, number of babies expected and any added risk factors.

viva.q: What three checks decide on warmer steps?
viva.a: Term birth, breathing or crying, and good tone; a no to any one means initial steps.

viva.q: What does TABC stand for?
viva.a: Temperature control, airway, breathing, and circulation with drugs.

image.brief: Close view of a newborn manikin face on a plain background with a small ventilation mask and a pulse oximeter probe on the right wrist.

credit.author: The original uploader was Bcatt at English Wikipedia.

items.summary: When to stimulate, when to ventilate, which oxygen to start with and how to track the response.

blocks.title: Tactile stimulation
bullets: After drying and positioning, flick the soles or rub the back gently to trigger breathing.

blocks.title: Deciding on ventilation
bullets: Judge breathing and heart rate rather than colour after the first handling.
If the rate is under 100 beats per minute, or the infant is apnoeic or gasping, begin positive pressure ventilation (PPV).
If the rate is above 100 with laboured breathing, consider continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), mainly in preterm infants.

blocks.title: Starting oxygen
bullets: Begin term resuscitation on 21 percent oxygen, which is room air.
Begin preterm resuscitation on 21 to 30 percent oxygen.

blocks.title: Monitoring the response
bullets: Recheck breathing, heart rate and oxygen saturation (SpO2) about every 30 seconds.
Use pulse oximetry and a three lead electrocardiogram (ECG) monitor for a fast reliable rate.
Place the oximeter probe on the right hand or wrist to read pre-ductal saturation.
Adjust added oxygen against the target pre-ductal values on the flow diagram for term and preterm alike.

viva.q: How do you give tactile stimulation?
viva.a: Flick the soles of the feet or give a gentle rub on the back after drying.

viva.q: When do you start positive pressure ventilation?
viva.a: When the heart rate is below 100 per minute or the baby is apnoeic or gasping.

viva.q: Where do you place the oximeter probe and why?
viva.a: On the right hand or wrist, because it reflects pre-ductal saturation.

title.en: Bag and mask ventilation and MR SOPA

image.brief: Side view of a newborn manikin on a plain background with a ventilation mask sealed over nose and mouth, showing jaw lift and bag squeeze.

credit.author: U.S. Navy photo by Emily McCamy

items.summary: Rate and pressure settings for mask ventilation, when it is indicated and the ordered MR SOPA fixes when air entry is poor.

blocks.title: Equipment, rate and pressure
bullets: Use a self inflating bag with a pressure gauge, reservoir, mask and metered oxygen source.
Ventilate 40 to 60 times per minute with the first breath at 30 to 40 cm of water, then 15 to 20.
A bag with reservoir and oxygen gives 100 percent; reservoir without oxygen gives 60 percent.
A bag with neither reservoir nor oxygen source gives 21 percent.

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Ventilate when breathing is absent or gasping.
Ventilate when the rate stays below 100 beats per minute even with breathing.
Ventilate for central cyanosis with low saturation that persists despite 100 percent free flow oxygen.

blocks.title: MR SOPA corrective steps
bullets: M: refit the mask to the face and ventilate again.
R: tilt the head to open the airway and try again.
S: clear the mouth and nose by suction.
O: open the mouth slightly, pull the jaw forward and ventilate again.
P: raise the pressure stepwise to a ceiling of 40 cm of water.
A: change to another airway such as a tracheal tube or laryngeal mask airway (LMA).

blocks.title: Contraindications and improvement
bullets: Avoid bag and mask ventilation in diaphragmatic hernia and in a limp meconium stained infant.
Improvement shows as a climbing heart rate, the start of own breaths and a rising SpO2.

viva.q: What rate and pressures do you use?
viva.a: 40 to 60 breaths a minute, first breath 30 to 40 cm of water, then 15 to 20.

viva.q: List the MR SOPA steps in order.
viva.a: Mask refit, reposition head, suction, open mouth with jaw lift, raise pressure, airway alternative.

viva.q: When is bag and mask ventilation contraindicated?
viva.a: In congenital diaphragmatic hernia and in non-vigorous meconium stained babies.

image.brief: Front view of a newborn manikin torso on a plain background showing two-thumb placement just below the line joining the nipples.

items.summary: When compressions may begin, where the hands go and the compression to breath rate to use.

blocks.title: When to start and stop
bullets: Good ventilation comes first: never compress without proven air entry shown by chest rise and breath sounds.
Start compressions if the rate stays below 60 beats per minute after 30 seconds of PPV with 100 percent oxygen.
Stop compressions once the rate climbs above 60 beats per minute.

blocks.title: Technique
bullets: Press the lower sternum just below the line joining the nipples.
Dip the chest by half to three quarters of an inch with each push.
Prefer the two thumb method with the fingers encircling the chest.
Give 90 compressions with 30 breaths each minute, chanting counts then a bag breath.

blocks.title: Older children
bullets: Between 1 and 8 years use a compression to breath ratio of 5 to 2.
Above 8 years use a ratio of 15 to 2.

viva.q: When do you start chest compressions in a newborn?
viva.a: Heart rate below 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with 100 percent oxygen.

viva.q: What rate and depth do you use?
viva.a: 90 compressions with 30 breaths a minute, pressing half to three quarters of an inch.

viva.q: Where do you place your thumbs?
viva.a: On the sternum just below the line between the nipples, using the two thumb grip.

image.brief: Side view of a newborn manikin head on a plain background with a laryngoscope blade lifting the tongue and a small tracheal tube beside it.

credit.author: No machine-readable author provided. Glow~commonswiki assumed (based on copyright claims).

items.summary: Reasons to pass a tracheal tube, the signs of correct placement and the CPAP settings for preterm infants.

blocks.title: Intubation method
bullets: Finish each attempt within 30 seconds; the older 20 second limit no longer applies.
Give no free flow oxygen to a non-breathing infant while the tube is being passed.
If intubation fails or is not feasible, place a laryngeal mask airway (LMA).

blocks.title: Indications
bullets: Intubate when positive pressure ventilation is needed for a long spell.
Intubate when mask ventilation does not move air, for tracheal suction or drugs, and in diaphragmatic hernia.

blocks.title: Signs of correct tube position
bullets: See the chest lift with every breath and hear air entry over both lung fields.
Check that the stomach does not swell with ventilation.
Watch for vapour fogging inside the tube during exhalation.
See the carbon dioxide detector change colour or read above 2 to 3 percent on exhalation.
Confirm the final position on X-ray.

blocks.title: CPAP and T-piece settings
bullets: Support a spontaneously breathing preterm under 32 weeks at risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) with 5 cm of water CPAP by T-piece once distress shows.
Infants needing ventilation receive peak and end pressures through a T-piece, starting at 15 over 5.
Raise the pressures only when rate and chest movement fail to improve quickly.

viva.q: How long may one intubation attempt take?
viva.a: Ideally within 30 seconds, not 20 seconds.

viva.q: Name four signs the tube is in the trachea.
viva.a: Chest rise, bilateral breath sounds, no gastric swelling and fogging or carbon dioxide change.

viva.q: What CPAP do you start in a preterm under 32 weeks?
viva.a: 5 cm of water by T-piece as soon as respiratory distress is noted.

title.en: Drugs and fluids in neonatal resuscitation

items.summary: Exact exam doses for epinephrine, naloxone and volume expanders, with when each is indicated.

blocks.title: Epinephrine
bullets: Give it when the rate stays below 60 beats per minute after 30 seconds of good ventilation plus 45 to 60 seconds more of compressions with ventilation.
Use a 1 to 10,000 solution, which holds 0.1 mg per ml.
Prefer the umbilical vein; the tracheal route may be used while venous access is secured.
Push rapidly: 0.1 to 0.3 ml per kg (0.01 to 0.03 mg per kg) intravenously in a 1 ml syringe.
Flush the line with 0.5 to 1 ml of normal saline after the intravenous dose.
By tube give 0.5 to 1 ml per kg (0.05 to 0.1 mg per kg) in a 3 to 6 ml syringe.
Reassess the rate about 1 minute later, waiting longer after a tracheal dose.
Repeat the dose every 3 to 5 minutes as needed.

blocks.title: Naloxone
bullets: Use it for depressed breathing when a narcotic was given within 4 hours of birth.
Give 0.1 mg per kg by vein, bone, tube or muscle.
Trial proof of safety and benefit is still lacking, with complication risks unclear.

blocks.title: Volume expanders
bullets: Give whole blood or normal saline 10 ml per kg intravenously for signs of hypovolaemia.
Ringer lactate is no longer advised for hypovolaemic shock.
Do not give sodium bicarbonate routinely to correct metabolic acidosis, as proof is lacking.

blocks.title: Dosage
bullets: Epinephrine intravenous: 0.1 to 0.3 ml per kg of 1 to 10,000 solution, flush 0.5 to 1 ml saline, repeat every 3 to 5 minutes.
Epinephrine tracheal: 0.5 to 1 ml per kg of 1 to 10,000 solution.
Naloxone: 0.1 mg per kg. Volume: 10 ml per kg normal saline or whole blood.

viva.q: When is epinephrine indicated?
viva.a: Heart rate below 60 after 30 seconds of ventilation plus 45 to 60 seconds of compressions with ventilation.

viva.q: What is the intravenous epinephrine dose?
viva.a: 0.1 to 0.3 ml per kg of 1 to 10,000 solution, flushed with 0.5 to 1 ml saline.

viva.q: What volume expander and dose do you use?
viva.a: Whole blood or normal saline 10 ml per kg intravenously for hypovolaemia.

items.summary: How long to wait before clamping the cord and why milking is not advised outside trials.

blocks.title: Delayed clamping
bullets: Wait one full minute before clamping in term and preterm infants who need no resuscitation.

blocks.title: Cord milking
bullets: Milking means stripping a 20 cm length of cord two to three times before clamping.
It moves placental blood across quickly and shows gains much like deferred clamping.
Because only small numbers have been studied, it is not advised outside a clinical trial.

viva.q: How long do you delay clamping in a baby needing no resuscitation?
viva.a: One minute, for both term and preterm infants.

viva.q: What is cord milking and is it recommended?
viva.a: Stripping 20 cm of cord two to three times; not recommended outside trials.

items.summary: The five-sign score recorded after birth, with when to repeat it and which value demands instant resuscitation.

head: Sign
Score 0
Score 1
Score 2
rows: Reflex irritability to a catheter in the nostril

blocks.title: Timing and action
bullets: Score the infant at 1, 5, 10 and 20 minutes until two successive totals reach 7 or more.
An infant scoring below 4 needs resuscitation at once.
Recall the parts as Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity and Respiratory effort.

viva.q: Name the five Apgar signs.
viva.a: Appearance or colour, pulse, grimace, activity or tone, and respiratory effort.

viva.q: When do you record the Apgar score?
viva.a: At 1, 5, 10 and 20 minutes until two successive scores of 7 or more.

viva.q: Which score demands immediate resuscitation?
viva.a: A total below 4.

title.en: Infant born through meconium stained liquor

image.brief: Front view of a newborn manikin under a radiant warmer on a plain background with a laryngoscope and suction catheter ready beside it.

items.summary: How to judge a meconium stained infant as vigorous or not and what to do for the limp baby.

blocks.title: Preparation
bullets: Treat each such birth as an emergency and keep two trained people ready for resuscitation.
When the liquor is stained, set out suction, warmer and airway kit before the birth.
Do not suck the mouth and nose at the perineum after the head is out but before the shoulders.

blocks.title: Vigorous or not
bullets: First decide vigour: a strong cry, rate above 100 per minute and good tone mean vigorous.
A vigorous infant needs routine care with the mother, not suction or intubation.

blocks.title: Care of the non-vigorous infant
bullets: Place the infant under a radiant warmer and hold back drying and suctioning that would stimulate.
Clear leftover meconium from the mouth and back of the throat under direct sight with a laryngoscope.
Begin positive pressure ventilation (PPV) promptly when breathing or rate remain poor.
Passing a tube for tracheal suction is no longer routine practice.
Use intubation with suction only as needed to secure oxygenation and ventilation.

viva.q: How do you define a vigorous meconium stained baby?
viva.a: Good cry, heart rate above 100 a minute and good muscle tone.

viva.q: Is suctioning at the perineum still advised?
viva.a: No. Intrapartum mouth and nose suction after the head is out is no longer recommended.

viva.q: How do you clear meconium in a limp baby?
viva.a: Under a warmer, suction mouth and pharynx under direct vision, then ventilate as needed.

items.summary: The expected age of appearance and fading for the primitive reflexes tested in early infancy.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Record each reflex as present, weak or absent with the infant's age at testing.
Persistence past the expected age or absence at the expected age needs review.

viva.q: When do palmar grasp and Moro appear and fade?
viva.a: Both appear by 32 weeks; palmar grasp fades by 3 months and Moro by 3 to 4 months.

viva.q: Which reflex never disappears?
viva.a: The parachute response, present from 9 months through life.

viva.q: When does the Landau reflex appear and fade?
viva.a: It appears at 9 months and fades by 24 months.

items.summary: Harmless skin, scalp, eye, breast and genital findings that students must not mistake for disease.

blocks.title: Skin and scalp
bullets: Blotchy red rash of erythema toxicum, tiny white milia and slate grey Mongolian spots are benign.
Pink nape marks called stork bites, fine peeling, cradle cap and small skin pits or sinuses settle alone.
Small white Epstein pearls on palate or prepuce and teeth present at birth need only review.

blocks.title: Eyes, breast and genitalia
bullets: Small subconjunctival bleeds clear without treatment.
Breast fullness, vaginal spotting or discharge and hymenal tags reflect maternal hormones.
Physiological phimosis in boys is the normal state at this age.

viva.q: Name three benign newborn rashes or marks.
viva.a: Erythema toxicum, milia and Mongolian spots, plus stork bites and peeling skin.

viva.q: What causes breast swelling and vaginal spotting?
viva.a: Maternal hormones crossing to the infant; both settle without treatment.

viva.q: What are Epstein pearls?
viva.a: Tiny white benign cysts on the palate or prepuce of a newborn.

items.summary: A six-sign score that grades breathing difficulty in the newborn, with the mild, moderate and severe bands.

blocks.title: Grading
bullets: A total below 5 means mild distress and 5 to 8 means moderate distress.
A total above 8 marks severe distress needing urgent support.

viva.q: Which six signs make up the Downe score?
viva.a: Rate, cyanosis, retractions, grunt, air entry and prematurity.

viva.q: How do you grade the total?
viva.a: Below 5 is mild, 5 to 8 moderate and above 8 severe.

viva.q: What rate scores 2?
viva.a: A respiratory rate above 80 per minute.

unsure: Source prints the severe band as below 8, which contradicts the 5 to 8 moderate band, so it was taken as above 8; source cyanosis wording is garbled and was rephrased, reviewer to confirm.

title.en: Human milk, cow milk and phases of breast milk

items.summary: How human milk differs from cow milk and how breast milk changes from colostrum to mature milk.

head: Constituent
Human milk
Cow milk
rows: 0.2 gm, iron lower but better absorbed
Low in vitamins D, K and C

head: Phase
Timing
Character
rows: Richer in antibodies, vitamins and protein, lower in fat
More fat and calories, less immunoglobulin and protein
More fat, protein and calories, fewer minerals
Thin fluid rich in protein, sugar and minerals that quenches thirst
Rich in fat that satisfies hunger

viva.q: How does human milk protein compare with cow milk?
viva.a: About 1.1 gm per 100 ml against 3.3 gm, with less casein, so it digests better.

viva.q: How does colostrum differ from mature milk?
viva.a: Colostrum in the first 4 days carries more antibodies and protein with less fat.

viva.q: What is the difference between foremilk and hind milk?
viva.a: Foremilk at the start is watery and quenches thirst; hind milk at the end is fatty and satisfies hunger.

unsure: Source prints protein and casein as run-together digits 1.10.4 and 3.32.7 and fats as 3.83 and 3.72, so the split into protein, casein and fat rows is an interpretation; mineral and copper wording is also garbled, reviewer to confirm.

items.summary: Telling caput from cephalhaematoma by feel and course, plus the risks and bedside tests for hip dysplasia.

blocks.title: Caput against cephalhaematoma
bullets: A caput has hazy edges, crosses suture lines and fades within 1 week.
A cephalhaematoma has sharp edges, stays within one bone plate and clears by about 6 weeks.

blocks.title: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)
bullets: Risk is higher in firstborn infants, girls who form 80 percent of cases, positive family history and breech feet first birth.
Use the Ortolani test, which brings a dislocated hip out, and the Barlow test, which pushes an unstable hip back.

viva.q: How do you tell caput from cephalhaematoma?
viva.a: Caput has ill defined margins and fades by 1 week; cephalhaematoma is sharply limited and fades by 6 weeks.

viva.q: Name the risk factors for hip dysplasia.
viva.a: Firstborn, female sex, family history and breech presentation.

viva.q: What do the Ortolani and Barlow tests do?
viva.a: Ortolani brings the hip out of dislocation and Barlow pushes it back.

items.summary: Why early jaundice is so common, the dermal zone guide, the danger flags and the three lines of treatment.

blocks.title: How common and why
bullets: Jaundice affects about 60 percent of term and 80 percent of preterm infants in week one.
Yellow colour shows once total serum bilirubin (TSB) passes 5 to 7 mg per dl, against above 2 in adults.
Three processes raise it: faster red cell breakdown, slow immature liver clearance and recycling through enterohepatic circulation (EHC).

blocks.title: Pathological jaundice
bullets: Yellow colour within the first 24 hours is always abnormal.
A daily climb above 5 mg per dl or persistence past 14 days is abnormal.
A direct fraction above 2 mg per dl or signs of acute brain injury and kernicterus are abnormal.
Think of haemolysis from blood group mismatch or enzyme lack such as glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
Think of collected blood such as a cephalhaematoma.

blocks.title: Treatment
bullets: Support breastfeeding, give blue light phototherapy and reserve exchange transfusion for severe cases.

viva.q: At what bilirubin does a newborn look yellow?
viva.a: Above 5 to 7 mg per dl, while adults show colour above 2.

viva.q: Name two flags of pathological jaundice.
viva.a: Onset within 24 hours and a daily rise above 5 mg per dl.

viva.q: What are the three treatments listed?
viva.a: Breastfeeding support, blue light phototherapy and exchange transfusion.
